source.title: Generalization and Memorization along the Learning Trajectory of Neural Language Models: A Geometric Account of Categorization
source.authors: Bo-Juan Wang; Holly E. Jenkins; E. Wonnacott

record.tranche_reason: Tests generalization and memorization over training in decoder-only Transformers on synthetic grammars, an extension to a different setting from random-label fitting.
record.gate_note: The study does not train on random labels, corrupted labels, shuffled pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs. Its results concern category-level generalization and compression of familiar versus held-out grammatical strings; these findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The experiments measure category generalization and exemplar-specific memorization on structured synthetic grammars. They do not measure fitting random labels, corrupted labels, or unstructured inputs, or compare real-label and noise-label learning. Random allocation of tokens to grammatical categories is not random labeling of training examples.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: category-level generalization develops early on these synthetic grammars, while later exemplar-specific memorization can compromise generalization, especially in larger models. The authors interpret this as evidence for categorization-driven language-model learning.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic structured grammars, interpolation-based representation analysis, and information-compression comparisons; it does not use random labels or the original random-label intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size and training stage change the reported later-stage generalization and memorization patterns.

fits_no_version.finding: Transformers develop category-sensitive interpolation responses early; prolonged training weakens these responses most strongly in the largest Study 1 model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On these synthetic grammars, category-level representation geometry emerges early and can weaken during prolonged training.

fits_no_version.finding: Familiar and held-out grammatical strings initially gain probability together. Larger models later favor familiar combinations more strongly, with sampled rankings reaching about 88% and nearly 100%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On this structured grammar task, generalization develops early, followed by increasing exemplar-specific memorization and poorer held-out performance in larger models.

record.problems: Main text reports only the first replicate for each model; the appendix states qualitative replication across three seeds. Results are largely qualitative descriptions of figures without numeric trajectory values or uncertainty estimates. The experiments use controlled synthetic grammars, not random labels or image data.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows beyond the reported model-specific results were omitted.

untested.parts: All parts: random-label training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
All parts: relative fitting time for random and true labels and convergence across corruption fractions.
All parts: fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
All parts: perfect training fit and test-error degradation across label-corruption fractions.
All parts. Setting dropout and weight decay to zero without a regularization comparison does not test their necessity or sufficiency.
Real-label versus noisy/random-label learning trajectories. Early grammatical generalization followed by exemplar-specific memorization does not establish this comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T3 classification conflicts with its correctly unlinked rows and not-tested version assessments. States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V6; this does not dispute the reported grammar-task effects. The appendix supplies qualitative three-seed replication, but no additional result tests a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting, chance test error, and whether architecture or hyperparameters must change.
Training time for random versus true labels and convergence as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test error across increasing fractions of randomly corrupted labels.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
The study compares generalization with exemplar-specific memorization on structured grammars, but does not compare learning real labels with learning noisy or random labels.

rows.operation_detail: Measured N- and Q-category probability mass for interpolated vectors between M and P embedding centres over training.

conditions.value: interpolated vectors between M and P centres

rows.measure: Category preference along the interpolation path
rows.baseline: At the beginning, there is no preference to N category or Q category.
rows.value: By iteration 550, vectors nearer M preferentially predicted N and vectors nearer P preferentially predicted Q; the intermediate vectors changed smoothly. The boundary strengthened by iterations 750-1,000 and remained stable through iteration 5,000.
rows.note: Qualitative description; precise values are shown in the figure.
rows.check: Interpolation-based category preference measures none of V1–V6.

rows.operation_detail: Measured correct target-category probability mass for observed MN and PQ test sequences over training.

conditions.value: observed MN and PQ test sequences

rows.value: The probability mass for the correct category gradually approached 1.
rows.note: The text reports the qualitative trajectory, not a final numeric value.
rows.check: Category prediction on held-out grammatical combinations measures none of V1–V6. The uniform category-probability baseline is 0.2.

rows.operation_detail: Measured N- and Q-category probability mass for interpolated vectors between M and P embedding centres over training.

conditions.value: interpolated vectors between M and P centres

rows.measure: Category preference along the interpolation path
rows.value: A smooth M-to-N and P-to-Q gradient was visible by iteration 400 and strongly established by iteration 700; later the global structure was gradually compromised but not totally destructed.
rows.note: Qualitative description; precise values are shown in the figure.
rows.check: Interpolation geometry measures none of V1–V6; its weakening cannot establish partial random-label fitting.

conditions.value: observed MN and PQ test sequences

rows.value: The model learned the dependencies perfectly at around 1,000 iterations; at a later stage, correct-category probability mass starts to drop.
rows.note: The text reports the qualitative trajectory, not numeric values.
rows.check: Held-out category prediction measures none of V1–V6. The uniform category-probability baseline is 0.2.

rows.operation_detail: Measured N- and Q-category probability mass for interpolated vectors between M and P embedding centres over training.

conditions.value: interpolated vectors between M and P centres

rows.measure: Category preference along the interpolation path
rows.value: A global geometric structure formed by iteration 300, was compromised by 76,000 iterations, and was totally destructed at a later stage.
rows.note: The later loss of the interpolation pattern contrasts with its early formation; precise values are shown in the figure.
rows.check: Loss of interpolation structure does not reverse any claim version. The main text describes complete destruction for the displayed run; the appendix describes weaker, fragmented responses across seeds.

rows.operation_detail: Measured correct target-category probability mass for observed MN and PQ test sequences over training.

conditions.value: observed MN and PQ test sequences

rows.value: At later stages, probability mass for the correct category remained high in observed-token analysis; the drop was more significant than in 4-4-32.
rows.note: Qualitative description; precise values are shown in the figure.
rows.check: Held-out category prediction measures none of V1–V6. The uniform category-probability baseline is 0.2; observed tokens here occur in previously unseen bigram combinations.

rows.operation_detail: Compared information-compression scores for familiar training-core strings and held-out test strings over training.

conditions.value: familiar training-core and held-out test strings

rows.measure: Mean information-compression score relative to the category-level reference
rows.value: Both trajectories decreased together toward the -14.51-bit reference during early learning; later, familiar and held-out scores remained close to the reference.
rows.note: The text describes trajectory shapes; exact plotted values are not provided.
rows.check: Compression of grammatical strings does not compare learning real labels with learning noisy or random labels.

rows.operation_detail: Compared information-compression scores for familiar training-core strings and held-out test strings over training.

conditions.value: familiar training-core and held-out test strings

rows.measure: Mean information-compression score relative to the category-level reference
rows.value: Both trajectories decreased together toward the reference during early learning; later, the familiar score fell below the reference while the held-out score gradually increased above it.
rows.note: The text describes trajectory shapes; exact plotted values are not provided.
rows.check: Familiar–held-out compression divergence measures exemplar-specific learning on structured data, not any listed version.

rows.operation_detail: Compared information-compression scores for familiar training-core strings and held-out test strings over training.

conditions.value: familiar training-core and held-out test strings

rows.measure: Mean information-compression score relative to the category-level reference
rows.value: Both trajectories decreased together toward the reference during early learning; later the familiar strings were progressively more compressed and held-out sequence compression increased substantially.
rows.note: The text describes trajectory shapes; exact plotted values are not provided.
rows.check: Measures none of V1–V6. Clarify the value: the held-out compression score increases substantially, meaning weaker compression and lower probability, while familiar strings receive stronger compression.

rows.operation_detail: Ranked sampled observed strings by information compression relative to held-out grammatical strings.
rows.measure: Mean percentage of observed strings more strongly compressed than each held-out string
rows.value: The sampled rank begins near 50%; the model remains only modestly above 50%.
rows.note: No exact later percentage is stated for this model.
rows.check: Ranking familiar against held-out grammatical strings does not measure real-label versus noise-label learning.

rows.operation_detail: Ranked sampled observed strings by information compression relative to held-out grammatical strings.

rows.value: The sampled rank begins near 50% and rises gradually to about 88%.
rows.note: The text says some held-out strings remain more strongly compressed.

rows.operation_detail: Ranked sampled observed strings by information compression relative to held-out grammatical strings.
rows.measure: Mean percentage of observed strings more strongly compressed than each held-out string
rows.value: The sampled rank begins near 50% and rapidly approaches 100% at later checkpoints.
rows.note: The authors describe this as almost all sampled observed strings being more strongly compressed at later checkpoints.
rows.check: The near-100% ranking measures preference for observed grammatical strings, not random-label fitting or noise-learning order.
